news_drafts.headline: Nottinghamshire to receive £35.8m in November for schools deficit; high needs forecast £68.8m over
news_drafts.lead:
Nottinghamshire County Council has been notified that government funding covering 90% of its dedicated schools grant (DSG) deficit at 31 March 2026 will be paid in November 2026. The sum is £35.8m, against a DSG deficit of £39.8m at the end of 2025/26. The DSG is the government grant that funds schools, and a deficit on it is an overspend on that grant. The council's Financial Monitoring Report says confirmation came after its SEND Reform Plan was submitted.

The same report, for period 5 of 2026/27, forecasts a £68.8m overspend for the year on the high needs block, the part of school funding for children with special educational needs and disabilities (SEND). The forecast is £207.7m of spending against a high needs budget of £138.9m. The paper says the underlying position continues to deteriorate, citing sustained demand and cost pressures in SEND services.

The council's Budget Update Report, also before Cabinet on 5 November, says arrangements for deficits arising in 2026/27 and 2027/28 have not yet been confirmed. It expects further announcements before the end of March 2028. It says continuation of 90% support cannot currently be assumed. If it is not sustained, the remaining 10%, £6.9m of the forecast 2026/27 high needs deficit, would have to be met from the council's reserves.

news_drafts.headline: Nottinghamshire: Ombudsman found fault in seven SEND cases as EHC Plan numbers rose 27% in a year
news_drafts.lead:
The Local Government and Social Care Ombudsman, the independent body that investigates complaints about councils, found fault in seven cases involving Nottinghamshire County Council's special educational needs and disabilities (SEND) service between March and September 2026. The decisions are set out in a paper for the council's Audit and Governance Committee, which meets on 14 October.

The paper describes the faults as systematic. They mainly concerned a failure to secure the support written into Education, Health and Care (EHC) Plans, the legal documents setting out what help a child with special needs must receive. Other faults were delays in the plan process and missed educational provision. In the paper's words: "A recurring theme was the failure to ensure that agreed educational or therapeutic provision was delivered. This included missed special school placements, physiotherapy, occupational therapy, music therapy, communication aids (AAC), and wider EHC provision."

Over the same period the number of EHC Plans in Nottinghamshire grew to just under 7,000, a rise of 27% on the previous year.
news_drafts.paper_title: Local Government and Social Care Ombudsman decisions – March - September 2026

news_drafts.headline: Nottinghamshire forecasts £68.82m schools-funding overspend; £35.8m relief awaits government decision
news_drafts.lead:
Nottinghamshire County Council expects to overspend its dedicated schools grant (the government grant that funds schools) by £68.82 million in 2026/27, according to a first-quarter performance and finance report to its Children and Families Select Committee. The paper says the overspend is "primarily driven by increased demand for Education, Health and Care Plan placements and use of independent specialist provision."

Independent specialist provision for children with Education, Health and Care Plans accounts for £52.6 million of the total. Spending on it is forecast at £74.9 million against a budget of £22.4 million. Post-16 provision is forecast to overspend by £7.9 million.

The council submitted its High Needs Reform Plan to the Department for Education in June 2026. High needs is the part of school funding for children with special educational needs and disabilities. If the department approves the plan, relief of 90 per cent of the schools-funding deficit held in reserves outside individual school budgets at 31 March 2026 would be made available. That deficit stood at £39.8 million, so the grant would be worth up to £35.823 million to the council. The paper says central government has not yet announced its decision, or how it will treat the 2026/27 overspend.

findings.paper_title: Police Reform - PCC Function Transfer to East Midlands Mayor
findings.headline: The English Devolution and Community Empowerment Act 2026 requires separate police funding components for each police area where one Mayor exercises PCC responsibilities across more than one force area.
findings.detail: The paper says the Act is intended to preserve transparency and accountability for police funding and precepts. Nottinghamshire and Derbyshire would be covered by a single East Midlands Mayor, so this requirement would apply to them.
findings.matters: A finance officer at a billing authority that collects the police precept would need to know how the precept and police funding will be separated by police area after the 2028 transfer.
findings.quote: the Act requires separate police funding components for each police area

findings.headline: The paper says the administration is being delivered within existing resources
findings.detail: The financial implications section states that the administration of the Nottinghamshire Pension Fund is being delivered within existing resources, and this is alongside the report's note on resourcing levels and backlogs.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council would want to know that the fund reports its administration cost as contained within budget while the backlog and staffing issues remain open.
findings.quote: The administration of the Nottinghamshire Pension Fund is being delivered within existing resources.

findings.headline: The report flags staff departures with considerable LGPS experience as a resourcing issue to be addressed
findings.detail: The paper lists the team's establishment and says apprentices became permanent members of the Administration Team on 1 October 2025. It states that the level of resources, particularly after departures of experienced staff, will need to be addressed going forward to build on services.
findings.matters: Staff recruitment shortfalls across the LGPS are a sector-wide pressure, and the paper ties the Fund's continued service levels to a resourcing decision it has yet to make.
findings.figures: 25.76 practitioners (30 people) in the Administration Team as at 31 March 2026
findings.quote: particularly with the departure of a number of staff with a considerable amount of LGPS experience is something that will need

findings.headline: Completed administrative processes rose 24.17% to 94,343 in 2025/26
findings.detail: The paper reports that total completed processes, including those outside the KPI measures, rose from 75,979 to 94,343. It attributes the increase to new requirements in complex legislation. The KPI-measured processes rose 6.33% to 18,307.
findings.matters: The fund's workload grew faster than its KPI-measured processes, which is the context a finance director needs when judging whether the team is keeping pace with regulatory change.
findings.figures: 94,343 processes completed (2025/26); 75,979 (2024/25); up 24.17%; KPI processes 18,307, up 6.33%
findings.quote: The number of tasks completed by the Team have increased over recent years

findings.headline: Pensioner membership rose to 51,931 in 2025/26 while active membership fell to 48,231
findings.detail: Pensioners rose from 49,323 to 51,931 over the year, and active members fell from 49,261 to 48,231. The paper also says the Fund continues to see an increase in the number of members retiring from active and deferred membership.
findings.matters: A growing pensioner base against a shrinking active base changes the balance of future pension payments and contributions, which affects the fund's cash flow and liability profile.
